submission.natural_language_explanation: A dense, weakly selective layer-4 direction that peaks (0.7-1.1 of max) on the closing piece of a multi-token unit that was built from a separate opening fragment: the second or later subword of a rare word or name split after a word-start fragment (' Sc'+'ro'+'oge', ' Nass'+'au', ' Ride'+'au', ' Stre'+'pt', ' transc'+'ends', ' subs'+'erv'+'ient', ' ind'+'istinguish'+'able', 'stri'+'pped'), and the second word of a fixed function-word frame (' no'+' matter', ' in order'+' for', ' for'+' any', ' to'+' fund', ' breaks'+' the'). The same words written as one whole token, word-initial fragments, punctuation and newlines stay low (below about 0.45), and many ordinary tokens sit at a 0.1-0.4 background.

rival_explanations: Pure token identity: a fixed set of tokens ('au', 'oge', ' any', ' fund', ' matter') fires wherever it appears; this predicts that ' the' after any verb and 'au' inside any word fire equally, whereas the hypothesis predicts that the context and the fragment before the token matter.

Any non-initial subword piece of any multi-token word fires; this broader reading predicts high activation on the inner pieces of words such as acetaminophen, Kalamazoo or mitochondria, where the hypothesis (and measurement, at most 0.35) predicts only a weak response.

The direction tracks how predictable the current token is from the previous one (the closing part of any strongly bound bigram or collocation), so it predicts that common idioms such as 'Baton Rouge' or 'New Orleans' fire as strongly as rare split words.
